title: Algorithmic and Psycholinguistic Specifications for Five-Phase Load-Smoothing Experiment
answer:
## Track 1: Projective Baseline Linearization Algorithm (Futrell et al. 2015)

The random projective linearization algorithm used by Futrell, Mahowald & Gibson (2015) originates from Gildea & Temperley (2010) [1, 7]. The procedure is recursive: starting at the root node of a dependency tree, collect the head word and its dependents and order them randomly, then repeat the process for each dependent [1]. More precisely, at each node the dependents are randomly partitioned into a left set and a right set, each set is randomly permuted, the left dependents are linearized recursively, then the head is placed, then the right dependents are linearized recursively [6, 7]. This is an UNCONSTRAINED projective baseline: each dependent is equally likely to appear on either side of its head, producing a uniform distribution over all projective orderings of the given dependency tree [1, 6].

The pseudocode is:
```
function LINEARIZE_SUBTREE(node):
  dependents = node.get_dependents()
  for dep in dependents:
    if random() < 0.5: left_set.append(dep)
    else: right_set.append(dep)
  shuffle(left_set); shuffle(right_set)
  result = []
  for dep in left_set: result.extend(LINEARIZE_SUBTREE(dep))
  result.append(node)
  for dep in right_set: result.extend(LINEARIZE_SUBTREE(dep))
  return result
```

Futrell et al. used 100 random linearization samples per sentence [1]. Dependency length is defined as the number of words between head and dependent (including the dependent), excluding punctuation and root arcs [1]. Sentences with length < 100 words were included in regression analysis, with DLM significance emerging at sentence length >= 12 across languages [1]. A second 'fixed word order' baseline assigns each dependency relation type a random weight in [-1, 1] and orders dependents by weight (head receives weight 0), creating a grammar-like baseline that maintains word order regularities within a sentence [1].

The code implementing these analyses is available at the Futrell/cliqs GitHub repository [8], which provides Python tools for comparing dependency length to random and minimal baselines. An alternative implementation exists at marinecourtin/Alearbres with an explicit `create_random_pj_linearisation` function.

For the optimized fixed-word-order grammar baseline, Gildea & Temperley (2007) achieved average dependency length per sentence of 42.5, fairly close to the 47.5 of original English text and much lower than the 82.7 of random baselines [7]. Temperley & Gildea (2018) provide a comprehensive review describing the algorithm in further detail [6].

**Caveat:** Liu (2015) criticized the projective-only baseline as understating DLM since projectivity itself is a DLM-related property [1]. The 100-sample Monte Carlo approach may underestimate variance for very long sentences; closed-form expectations exist but Futrell et al. chose Monte Carlo [6].

---

## Track 2: Intervener Complexity (IC) Definition and Yadav et al. 2022 Methodology

Yadav, Mittal & Husain (2022) define intervener complexity (IC) as the number of syntactic heads that intervene a dependency [2]. Specifically, for a dependency arc from word d (dependent) to word h (head), IC is the count of words w in linear positions between d and h such that w is the HEAD of at least one other dependency (i.e., w has >= 1 dependent in the tree) [2]. This counts structurally prominent interveners, not all intervening tokens.

This definition differs from Gibson's (2000) Dependency Locality Theory (DLT), which counts new discourse referents (nouns and verbs) intervening between head and dependent [20]. In Gibson's DLT, the integration cost of a word is a function of the number of new discourse referents that intervene between the two items of a dependency, where full NPs introduce new discourse referents but pronouns do not [20]. By contrast, Yadav et al.'s IC counts any word that serves as a syntactic head regardless of its lexical category [2].

The study used 54 Surface-Syntactic Universal Dependencies (SUD) version 2.4 treebanks [2]. Critically, they used SUD rather than standard UD. In SUD, function words are dependents of content words following distributional criteria for headedness, whereas in standard UD, function words (prepositions, auxiliaries) can be syntactic heads [16]. This means SUD will count fewer function-word heads as interveners, directly affecting IC computation. SUD and UD are near-isomorphic and can be converted bidirectionally using rule-based graph transformation grammars [16]. Treebanks with < 500 sentences and ancient languages (Latin, Old Greek, Sanskrit, Old Church Slavonic, Old Russian, Old French) were excluded [2]. Sentences were restricted to length <= 12 words due to computational constraints of rejection sampling for the most constrained baselines [2].

The tree properties controlled were: sentence length (number of nodes), crossing dependencies, node arity (number of dependents), tree depth (max root-to-leaf distance), dependency length sequence, and IC sequence [2].

Six baselines were generated via rejection sampling [2]: (1) Random structures sampled via Prufer codes, matched on sentence length + crossing dependencies; (2) Random linear arrangements (RLA) preserving dependency relations, matched on topology + crossings; (3) DL-matched random structures constrained to match real trees' dependency length sequence; (4) DL-matched RLAs; (5) IC-matched random structures constrained to match real trees' IC sequence; (6) IC-matched RLAs matched on IC sequence + topology [2].

The statistical models were linear mixed-effects models (lme4 in R): IC_ij = beta_0 + u_0j + (beta_1 + u_1j)*S_ij + (beta_2 + u_2j)*R_ij + (beta_3 + u_3j)*S_ij*R_ij + epsilon, where IC_ij/DL_ij is the mean IC or dependency length for sentence i in language j, S_ij is sentence length, R_ij is a dummy variable (1=real, 0=baseline), and beta_3 (the interaction) is the key coefficient of interest [2]. Negative beta_3 means real trees grow slower than baselines, supporting minimization.

**Critical results on DLM disappearance [2]:**
- ICM vs random structures: beta3 = -0.17, t = -24.5 (IC is minimized, significant)
- ICM vs RLAs: beta3 = -0.13, t = -19.7 (IC is minimized, significant)
- ICM independent of DL (DL-matched RS): beta3 = -0.03, t = -6.4 (IC still minimized even after DL control)
- ICM independent of DL (DL-matched RLAs): beta3 = -0.02, t = -4.8 (IC still minimized)
- DLM independent of IC (IC-matched RS): beta3 = -0.07, t = -12.9 (DL still minimized vs structures)
- **DLM independent of IC (IC-matched RLAs): beta3 = 0.01, t = 3.5 (DL is NOT minimized when IC + topology controlled)** [2]

This means traditional word-count DLM appears epiphenomenal to intervener complexity minimization when tree structure is held constant [2]. IC minimization survives all controls, but DLM vanishes entirely when IC-matched random linear arrangements control for both IC and topology [2].

Dyer (2023) replicated on 35 languages using a parallel corpus (PUD), confirming both DLM and ICM but finding a markedly lesser extent of both in verb-final languages, suggesting further research is needed on this asymmetry [21].

---

## Track 3: Psycholinguistic Evidence for Cognitive Cost Convexity (alpha Estimation)

### ACT-R Fan Effect

In the Lewis & Vasishth (2005) ACT-R model of sentence processing [5], the activation of chunk i is: A_i = B_i + sum_j(W_j * S_ji), where B_i is base-level activation, W_j is the attentional weight for source j (typically W = source_activation / num_sources), and S_ji is the associative strength from cue j to chunk i [5, 9]. The base-level activation follows a power-law decay: B_i = ln(sum_k(t_k^{-d})) where d ~ 0.5 is the decay rate [9]. The fan effect enters through the associative strength: S_ji = S - ln(fan_j), where S ~ 1.6 is the maximum associative strength and fan_j is the number of chunks associated with cue j [9]. Retrieval time is: T = F * exp(-A_i), where F ~ 0.63 is the latency factor [5, 9].

Default ACT-R parameter values include: F (latency factor) ~ 0.35-1.0 (typically 0.63), d (decay) ~ 0.5, S (max association) ~ 1.6-2.0, and s (noise) ~ 0.12-0.5 [9].

The scaling derivation for concurrent dependencies proceeds as follows: With fan = n items sharing a cue, S_ji = S - ln(n), so A = B + W*(S - ln(n)), giving T = F * exp(-B - WS + W*ln(n)) = F * exp(-B-WS) * n^W [5, 9]. Thus retrieval time for a single item scales as n^W. For the total concurrent load with n open dependencies (as in the IMB scenario), total processing cost ~ n * T(n) = C * n^(1+W) [5, 9]. With 2 retrieval cues (W = 0.5): alpha ~ 1.5. With 1 retrieval cue (W = 1.0): alpha ~ 2.0. This directly motivates testing alpha = 1.5 and alpha = 2.0 in the experiment.

Engelmann, Jager & Vasishth (2019) extended the Lewis & Vasishth model with prominence effects and variable cue-feature associations, finding that the original model has only partial success and that prominence modulations are needed to explain all interference patterns [18].

### Center-Embedding Difficulty

Center-embedded sentences become catastrophically difficult at embedding depth >= 2 [23]. The classic example from Miller & Chomsky (1963) is 'The rat the cat the dog chased ate died' [23]. Karlsson (2007) provided empirical evidence that the maximum degree of multiple center-embedding of clauses is exactly 3 in written language, with thirteen genuine examples across Indo-European languages [23]. Lewis & Vasishth (2005) explained center-embedding difficulty through their ACT-R model: at depth 2+, retrieval cues become non-discriminating, causing massive interference between similar items in memory [5]. The catastrophic failure at depth 2-3 implies cost growth is at minimum quadratic (alpha >= 2) or possibly exponential [5, 23].

**Caveat:** Center-embedding difficulty conflates storage cost, retrieval interference, and similarity-based confusion. The alpha parameter in IMB maps to instantaneous load magnitude, which is related but not identical to embedding depth.

### Similarity-Based Interference

Gordon, Hendrick & Levine (2002) demonstrated that similarity between noun phrases modulates processing difficulty in syntactically complex sentences [10]. When intervening NPs are of the same type (e.g., both common nouns), difficulty increases substantially; when they are dissimilar (e.g., names vs. nouns), the difficulty is reduced or eliminated [10]. This shows that syntactic processing relies on working memory resources susceptible to similarity-based interference [10]. The interference effect is consistent with superlinear cost scaling but without precise quantification of the exponent.

### Surprisal Scaling Debate

The relationship between surprisal and reading time is debated. Smith & Levy (2013) and Shain et al. (2022) found evidence for a linear relationship, while Meister et al. (2021) and Hoover et al. (2022) found superlinear effects, especially with better language models. Futrell, Gibson & Levy (2020) unified surprisal theory and memory-based theories into a single framework via lossy-context surprisal, showing that dependency locality effects can be derived as a special case of a more general information locality principle [19]. This debate concerns the surprisal-to-RT mapping rather than the IMB cost function directly, but superlinear surprisal effects independently motivate alpha > 1.

### Alpha Grid Assessment

The proposed grid {1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0} is well-motivated [5, 9, 23]:
- alpha = 1.0: Linear cost, zero load-smoothing benefit. Critical NEGATIVE CONTROL. If load smoothing is real, alpha=1.0 should show the weakest effect.
- alpha = 1.2: Mild superlinearity. Tests whether even weak convexity produces detectable smoothing.
- alpha = 1.5: ACT-R fan prediction with 2 retrieval cues (W=0.5). Moderate superlinearity.
- alpha = 2.0: ACT-R fan prediction with 1 retrieval cue (W=1.0). Quadratic cost. Also consistent with center-embedding difficulty threshold.
- alpha = 3.0: Strong superlinearity. Tests whether very steep cost functions produce even stronger smoothing signals. Upper bound of plausible range.

No existing study was found that directly estimates alpha empirically from reading time data by fitting IMB^alpha, making this a novel contribution of the proposed experiment.

---

## Track 4: Complete Spoken vs. Written UD Treebank Pairs

Based on a systematic review of spoken UD treebanks [4, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 22, 24, 25], five viable spoken-written pairs were identified for the modality comparison experiment:

**1. Slovenian: sl_sst (spoken) vs sl_ssj (written) -- EXCELLENT** [11]
The Spoken Slovenian Treebank (SST) contains 6,121 utterances and 98,393 tokens of spontaneous speech across 344 speech events (~10 hours), including monologic, dialogic, and multi-party conversations [11]. Extended in UD v2.14 with GOS v2 data (parliamentary debates, round tables, online events) [11, 22]. The UD v2.15 release (November 2024) further updated this treebank [22]. Annotation follows guidelines by Dobrovoljc & Nivre (2016) and Dobrovoljc (2022), with reparandum, discourse:filler, parataxis:restart, and parataxis:discourse relations for spoken phenomena [11]. Same annotation team as sl_ssj, making this the most directly comparable pair.

**2. French: fr_rhapsodie (spoken) vs fr_gsd (written) -- GOOD** [12]
The French Rhapsodie treebank contains 3,209 sentences and 43,699 tokens of spoken French [12]. Derived from the Rhapsodie prosodic-syntactic treebank (~3 hours of speech). Has reparandum and parataxis:insert relations [12]. Different annotation origins from fr_gsd, but both converted to UD standards. Size imbalance (spoken much smaller than written ~400K tokens).

**3. Norwegian: no_nynorsklia (spoken) vs no_nynorsk (written) -- MODERATE** [14]
The Norwegian NynorskLIA treebank contains 5,250 sentences and 55,410 tokens from dialect recordings made between 1950-1990, digitized and transcribed [14]. Morphosyntactic annotation follows the Norwegian Dependency Treebank framework extended for spoken phenomena (repairs, deletions) [14]. Dialect vs. standard language mismatch and historical nature are caveats.

**4. Hebrew: he_iahltknesset (spoken) vs he_iahltwiki (written) -- MODERATE** [24, 22]
The Hebrew IAHLTknesset treebank is a new treebank introduced in UD v2.15 (November 2024), containing approximately 2,800 sentences and 67,007 tokens from transcribed Israeli Knesset parliamentary proceedings [24, 22]. Same IAHLT annotation scheme as he_iahltwiki. Caveat: parliamentary speech is formal, limiting the spoken-written contrast.

**5. Czech: cs_pdtc/PDTSC (spoken) vs cs_pdt (written) -- CONDITIONAL** [15]
The Czech PDTC consolidated treebank contains 213,897 sentences and 3,432,078 tokens across four sub-corpora, including PDTSC (Prague Dependency Treebank of Spoken Czech) with spontaneous dialog transcriptions from the Malach and Companions projects [15]. The spoken portion must be filtered by genre metadata. Shared annotation framework (PDT-style converted to UD).

**Pairs excluded:**
- Spanish es_coser: Only 539 sentences and 7,987 tokens of rural dialectal speech -- too small for reliable analysis [13].
- Naija pcm_nsc: Large spoken treebank (9,242 sentences, 140,729 tokens) but no written Naija counterpart in UD [25].

**Additional spoken treebanks without clean written pairs** include Cantonese HK, Komi Zyrian IKDP (tiny dialectal corpus), Frisian Dutch Fame (400 sentences, code-switching), Turkish-German SAGT (2,184 sentences, code-switching), Abaza ATB (98 sentences), Chukchi HSE, and Beja Autogramm (11,951 tokens, replaced Beja NSC in v2.15) [4, 22].

Dobrovoljc (2022) found that spoken UD treebanks differ considerably in the inventory and format of transcribed phenomena, and in the principles adopted for morphosyntactic annotation [4]. This is particularly true for disfluency annotation where conflicting data suggest underspecification of the reparandum relation guidelines [4]. Key spoken-specific relations include: reparandum (self-repairs, present in sl_sst, fr_rhapsodie, es_coser, no_nynorsklia), discourse:filler (filled pauses, in sl_sst, es_coser), parataxis:restart (false starts, in sl_sst), and parataxis:insert (parentheticals, in fr_rhapsodie) [4, 11, 12, 13].

---

## Track 5: Clark et al. 2023 UID Methodology for LLF/UID Distinction

Clark, Meister, Pimentel, Hahn, Cotterell, Futrell & Levy (2023) tested whether uniform information density (UID) has influenced word order patterns cross-linguistically [3]. They studied 10 typologically diverse languages using two UID metrics [3]:

- **UIDv (Surprisal variance):** Var(surprisal(w_i | w_1...w_{i-1})) computed across all words in a sentence. Lower variance indicates more uniform information density [3].
- **UIDlv (Local variation):** Mean squared word-to-word change in surprisal: (1/(n-1)) * sum_{i=2}^{n} (surprisal(w_i) - surprisal(w_{i-1}))^2. Captures local smoothness of information flow [3].

Surprisal was computed using Transformer language models trained separately for each language using fairseq (architecture: transformer_lm), with training data from Wiki40b and CC100 corpora [3, 17]. Each language received its own dedicated language model rather than using a single multilingual model [17]. The training hyperparameters are specified in the repository's `data/train_model_transformer.sh` file [17].

Counterfactual word orders were generated using the formalism of Hahn et al. (2020), in which weights are assigned to each dependency relation type in the Universal Dependencies paradigm, and these weights are then used to linearize the hierarchical structure of a sentence's dependency parse [3, 17]. 'Reverse' orders negate all relation-type weights, producing mirror-image word orders (e.g., SVO becomes OVS) [3]. 'Linguistically implausible' counterfactuals correspond to word order patterns not attested in any known natural language [3].

Key findings include: (i) among SVO languages, real word orders consistently have greater information uniformity than reverse word orders; (ii) only linguistically implausible counterfactual orders consistently exceed the uniformity of real orders; (iii) counterfactual orders placing verbs before objects are more uniform than those placing objects before verbs in nearly every language [3].

### LLF vs. UID: Critical Distinction

Both Load Leveling (LLF) and UID are uniformity hypotheses about language structure, but they optimize fundamentally different quantities [3, 19, 20]:

- **UID** optimizes INFORMATION CONTENT uniformity: the variance of per-word surprisal (predictability) should be minimized across sentence positions [3].
- **LLF** optimizes MEMORY BURDEN uniformity: the variance of instantaneous memory burden (number of concurrent open dependencies, raised to power alpha) should be minimized across sentence positions.

They are orthogonal predictions: UID predicts word ORDER choices that smooth surprisal, while LLF predicts dependency ARRANGEMENT choices that smooth concurrent memory load [3, 19]. A sentence can satisfy UID perfectly (uniform surprisal) while violating LLF (highly variable IMB) if predictable words happen to co-occur with many open dependencies. Conversely, a sentence with smooth IMB may have highly variable surprisal.

Critically, LLF is purely structural (depends only on the dependency tree shape and linearization), while UID is lexical/distributional (depends on word probabilities in context) [3, 17]. LLF requires only the dependency parse to compute IMB, whereas UID requires a language model to estimate surprisal. This makes LLF more directly testable from treebank data alone.

Futrell, Gibson & Levy (2020) unified surprisal and memory-based theories through lossy-context surprisal, showing that dependency locality effects emerge from Bayesian updating with lossy memory representations [19]. Futrell, Levy & Gibson (2020) provided large-scale corpus evidence that dependency locality predicts word order in both grammar and usage beyond independently motivated principles [20]. These works establish the theoretical bridge between information-theoretic and memory-cost perspectives that the LLF experiment extends.

---

## Important Note on SUD vs. UD

Yadav et al. (2022) used SUD treebanks [2, 16]. In standard UD, content words are always heads (function words like prepositions and auxiliaries are dependents) [16]. In SUD, headedness follows distributional criteria, so function words that determine the distribution of a phrase can be heads [16]. This directly impacts IC computation: the set of 'heads' (words with dependents) differs between UD and SUD. If the LLF experiment uses UD treebanks, IC computation will differ from Yadav et al. The experiment should either (a) use SUD treebanks for strict comparability, or (b) use UD treebanks but test both and document the difference [2, 16].

sources.title: Futrell, Mahowald & Gibson (2015). Large-scale evidence of dependency length minimization in 37 languages. PNAS.

sources.summary: Core source for IC definition (count of syntactic heads between head and dependent), six rejection-sampled baselines, mixed-effects model specifications across 54 SUD v2.4 treebanks, and the critical finding that DLM vanishes (beta3=0.01) when IC and topology are controlled via IC-matched RLAs.

sources.title: Temperley & Gildea (2018). Minimizing Syntactic Dependency Lengths: Typological/Cognitive Universal?
sources.summary: Comprehensive review chapter describing the random projective linearization algorithm in detail: at each node, randomly assign each dependent to left or right of head, randomly order within each side, recurse into subtrees.

sources.title: Gordon, Hendrick & Levine (2002). Memory-Load Interference in Syntactic Processing. Psychological Science 13(5):425-430.
sources.summary: Key experimental evidence that similarity between NPs modulates processing difficulty: matched types (both common nouns) increase interference in object-extracted clefts, while dissimilar types (names vs nouns) reduce difficulty, showing non-modular working memory in syntax.

follow_up_questions: What is the exact list of 10 languages in Clark et al. (2023), and what per-language Transformer LM architectures and training hyperparameters were used? The full PDF was not accessible for detailed extraction.
Can the PDTSC spoken portion of the Czech cs_pdtc treebank be reliably isolated by genre metadata fields, and what is its exact size in sentences and tokens for the spoken-only subset?

Has anyone attempted to estimate the cost convexity exponent alpha empirically from reading time data, e.g., by fitting IMB^alpha to self-paced reading times across different dependency load configurations and comparing model fit across alpha values?
summary: This research delivers executable algorithmic specifications for all five phases of the Parametric Convex-Cost Load Smoothing experiment. Track 1 establishes the Futrell et al. (2015) projective baseline as a recursive Gildea-Temperley algorithm producing uniform projective orderings with 100 Monte Carlo samples. Track 2 extracts the full Yadav et al. (2022) methodology showing IC counts syntactic heads between head-dependent across 54 SUD treebanks, with DLM vanishing entirely when IC+topology are controlled. Track 3 derives alpha estimates from ACT-R fan effect math yielding alpha in [1.5, 2.0], supported by center-embedding and interference evidence, validating the grid {1.0,1.2,1.5,2.0,3.0}. Track 4 identifies five viable spoken-written UD treebank pairs led by Slovenian sl_sst/sl_ssj (best comparability). Track 5 specifies Clark et al. UID methodology and articulates LLF-UID orthogonality.
